name: Profit, Loss & Discount
intro: **Profit % is always on CP; discount % is always on MP.** Half the errors in this topic are a correct percentage applied to the wrong base (§2).
Chain everything as factors: markup, discount and wastage each multiply, and they act on different quantities (§12).

sets.name: Cost price, selling price and profit percent

qs.q: An article bought for ₹640 is sold for ₹768. Find the profit percent.
qs.h: §1 — profit % is on CP. 128/640.

qs.q: An article sold for ₹450 gives a 25% profit. Its cost price is
qs.h: §3 — divide by 1.25. Subtracting 25% of the SP is the planted error.

qs.q: A man sells an article at a 15% loss for ₹1,020. Find the cost price (in ₹).
qs.h: §3 — a 15% loss means SP = 0.85 × CP.

qs.q: If the cost price of 20 articles equals the selling price of 16 articles, the profit percent is
qs.h: §9 — the larger number sits on the CP side, so it's a profit. SP/CP = 20/16.

qs.q: By selling an article for ₹900 a man loses 10%. At what price should he sell it to gain 20% (in ₹)?
qs.h: §1 — recover CP first. Every profit or loss percentage refers back to that one number.

qs.q: A trader's profit is 25% of the cost price. His profit as a percentage of the selling price is
qs.h: §2 — the base changes from CP to SP. Take CP = 100.

sets.name: Marked price and a single discount

qs.q: An article marked at ₹1,500 is sold at a 12% discount. Find the selling price (in ₹).
qs.h: §4 — discount is on MP, always.

qs.q: A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost and allows a 25% discount. His profit percent is
qs.h: §4 — chain 1.4 and 0.75. The markup and the discount act on different bases, so they never simply subtract.

qs.q: A shopkeeper wants a 20% profit after allowing a 20% discount. By what percent above cost must he mark his goods?
qs.h: §4 read backwards — markup factor = (profit factor)/(discount factor).
qs.s: 1.2/0.8 = 1.5 ⟹ mark up by 50%. (Answering 40% assumes the two 20%s cancel.)

qs.q: An article marked at ₹800 is sold for ₹680. The rate of discount is
qs.h: §4 — divide the discount by the MP, not by the SP. One option is the SP-based answer.

qs.q: A shopkeeper marks an article 30% above cost and gives a discount, ending with a 4% profit. Find the discount percent.
qs.h: §4 — the discount factor is (profit factor)/(markup factor).

qs.q: Successive discounts of 20% and 10% are equivalent to a single discount of
qs.h: §5 — 0.8 × 0.9. The naive sum 30% is planted.

qs.q: An article marked at ₹2,500 is sold after successive discounts of 20%, 10% and 5%. Find the selling price (in ₹).
qs.h: §5 — chain all three factors, then multiply once.

qs.q: Which is the better deal for a buyer: a single discount of 30%, or successive discounts of 20% and 10%?
qs.h: §5 — compare the surviving factors 0.70 and 0.72. Smaller is better for the buyer.
qs.s: 0.70 vs 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 ⟹ the single 30% discount is better. Successive discounts always undershoot their sum.

qs.q: Successive discounts of 25% and x% are equivalent to a single discount of 40%. Find x.
qs.h: §5 — set 0.75 × (1 − x/100) = 0.60 and solve for the second factor.

qs.q: After two equal successive discounts, an article marked at ₹10,000 sells for ₹8,100. Each discount is
qs.h: §5 — 0.81 is a perfect square. Take the square root of the surviving factor.
qs.s: (1 − d)² = 0.81 ⟹ 1 − d = 0.9 ⟹ each discount is 10%. (19% is the single equivalent discount, planted.)

qs.q: A man sells two articles at ₹960 each, gaining 20% on one and losing 20% on the other. Overall he
qs.h: §6 — same SP with equal ± percentages is always a loss of x²/100 percent. Never a break-even.
qs.s: Loss = 20²/100 = 4%. (CPs are ₹800 and ₹1,200, total ₹2,000 against an SP of ₹1,920.)

qs.q: A man sells two horses at ₹4,000 each, gaining 25% on one and losing 25% on the other. Find his net loss (in ₹), to two decimals.
qs.h: §6 — the percentage loss is 25²/100 = 6.25%, but the question asks for the rupee amount, so find both CPs.

qs.q: An article is sold at a 20% profit. Had it been bought for 20% less and sold for ₹90 less, the profit would have been 25%. The original cost price was
qs.h: §6 — write both scenarios in terms of the same C and equate. Only one unknown is needed.
qs.s: 1.2C − 90 = 1.25(0.8C) = C ⟹ 0.2C = 90 ⟹ C = ₹450. Check: SP 540 vs new CP 360 and new SP 450 = 25% profit ✓

qs.q: By selling an article at ₹720 a man loses as much as he would gain by selling it at ₹880. Find the cost price (in ₹).
qs.h: §6 — equal rupee loss and gain means the CP is exactly midway.

qs.q: If the selling price of 10 articles equals the cost price of 12 articles, the profit percent is
qs.h: §9 — here the larger number is on the CP side, so it is a profit. SP/CP = 12/10.
qs.s: 10 SP = 12 CP ⟹ SP/CP = 1.2 ⟹ profit = 20%. (Reading it as 10/12 gives a 16.67% loss — the direction trap.)

qs.q: A shopkeeper sells at cost price but uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Find his profit percent, to two decimals.
qs.h: §7 — the base is what he actually gives, not what he claims. 100/900, not 100/1000.
qs.s: He gains 100 g on a true cost of 900 g ⟹ 100/900 = 11.11%. (10% uses the wrong base.)

qs.q: A dealer professes to sell at cost price but uses an 800 g weight for a kilogram. His gain is
A shopkeeper uses a 950 g weight for 1 kg and also marks up his goods 20%. Find his overall profit percent, to two decimals.
qs.h: §7 + §12 — the markup and the short weight are independent factors, so multiply them.
qs.s: 1.2 × (1000/950) = 1.2 × 1.05263 = 1.26316 ⟹ 26.32%. (Adding 20 + 5.26 gives 25.26% — close enough to be a plausible wrong answer.)

qs.q: Milk costing ₹40/litre is mixed with water and the mixture sold at ₹40/litre, yielding a 25% profit. The ratio of water to milk in the mixture is
qs.h: §8 — the base is the pure quantity, not the mixture. Water is free, so profit % = water/milk.
qs.s: Profit 25% = 1/4 ⟹ water : milk = 1 : 4. Check: 4 L milk costs ₹160, 5 L sells for ₹200, profit 40/160 = 25% ✓

qs.q: A milkman mixes water with milk and sells the mixture at cost price, making a 20% profit. Find the percentage of water in the mixture, to two decimals.
qs.h: §8 — 20% profit gives water : milk = 1 : 5, but the question asks for water as a share of the mixture.
qs.s: Water : milk = 1 : 5 ⟹ water as a fraction of the 6-part mixture = 1/6 = 16.67%. (Answering 20% confuses the two bases.)

sets.name: Equating goods, bulk offers and combined chains

qs.q: "Buy 3 get 1 free" is equivalent to a discount of
qs.h: §10 — the base is what you receive (4 items), not what you pay for (3).
qs.s: You get 4 for the price of 3 ⟹ 1/4 = 25%. (33.33% uses 3 as the base — the planted error.)

qs.q: A shop offers "buy 4 get 2 free". Find the equivalent discount percent, to two decimals.
qs.h: §10 — 2 free out of the 6 you take home.

qs.q: If the cost price of 15 articles equals the selling price of 12 articles, then there is a
qs.h: §9 — larger number on the CP side means a profit. Then SP/CP = 15/12.

qs.q: A shopkeeper marks his goods 50% above cost, allows a 20% discount, and finds 10% of his stock spoils and cannot be sold. Find his overall profit percent.
qs.h: §12 — markup and discount act on the price; wastage acts on the quantity. Assume 100 units at ₹1 each.
qs.s: Cost = ₹100. He sells 90 units at 1.5 × 0.8 = ₹1.20 each = ₹108 ⟹ profit = 8%.

qs.q: A trader sells two items at the same price, one at a 25% profit and the other at a 25% loss, with an overall loss of ₹500. His total selling price was
qs.h: §6 + §11 — the loss is 6.25% of the total CP, and the total CP is expressible in terms of the common SP.
qs.s: With each SP = x: CPs are 0.8x and (4/3)x ⟹ total CP = (32/15)x against total SP = 2x ⟹ loss = (2/15)x = 500 ⟹ x = ₹3,750 ⟹ total SP = ₹7,500.

qs.q: A shopkeeper marks goods 25% above cost and allows a 10% discount. His profit percent is
qs.h: Chain 1.25 and 0.9.

qs.q: An article costing ₹2,400 is sold at a 15% loss. Find the selling price (in ₹).
qs.h: Loss is on CP.

qs.q: Successive discounts of 10%, 20% and 25% are equivalent to a single discount of
qs.h: Chain all three factors.

qs.q: A dishonest trader sells at cost price but gives 750 g for 1 kg. Find his profit percent, to two decimals.
qs.h: The base is the 750 g he actually gives.

qs.q: A man buys 60 apples for ₹300 and sells them at 5 for ₹30. His profit percent is
qs.h: Put both sides on the same 60 apples.

qs.q: A shopkeeper wants a 25% profit after giving a 20% discount on the marked price. By what percent above cost must he mark the goods?
qs.h: Markup factor = profit factor ÷ discount factor.

qs.q: Two articles are sold at ₹1,200 each, one at a 20% profit and the other at a 20% loss. The net result is
qs.h: The percentage is 4%; convert it to rupees via the total CP.
qs.s: CPs = ₹1,000 and ₹1,500 ⟹ total CP ₹2,500 against SP ₹2,400 ⟹ a loss of ₹100 (4% ✓).

qs.q: By selling 45 lemons for ₹40 a man loses 20%. How many lemons must he sell for ₹24 to gain 20%?
qs.h: Work per lemon: SP, then CP, then the new SP.

qs.q: The marked price of an article is 20% above its cost price. After a discount the trader still makes a 2% profit. The discount is
qs.h: Discount factor = profit factor ÷ markup factor.

qs.q: A man buys milk at ₹30/litre, adds water, and sells the mixture at ₹36/litre for a 50% profit. Find the litres of water added per litre of milk.
qs.h: Water is free, so the cost stays at ₹30 per litre of milk.
qs.s: Per litre of milk: cost ₹30, required revenue ₹45 ⟹ mixture volume = 45/36 = 1.25 L ⟹ water = 0.25 litres.

audit: applying a percentage to the wrong base — profit is on CP, discount is on MP (§2)
getting the direction wrong when equating goods; the larger number's side decides profit vs loss (§9)
treating markup and discount as cancelling because the percentages match — the bases differ (§4)
adding successive discounts instead of chaining the factors (§5)
C5
reporting the combined discount where each individual one was asked
assuming equal ± percentages on the same SP break even; it is always an x²/100 loss (§6)
D3
introducing two unknowns where one C carries both scenarios
dividing the short weight's gain by 1000 instead of by what was actually given (§7)
E4, E5
using the mixture as the base where the pure quantity is the base, or vice versa (§8)
F1, F2
using the number paid for as the base instead of the number received (§10)
F4
applying wastage to the price rather than to the quantity sold (§12)
abandoning per-unit working, which is what keeps these two tractable
